findings.evidence: "The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter."
findings.fix: Merge the two "Overview"-style sections into one and state a single owner and a single publication cadence for the reimbursement log.
findings.violation: The document later states in the "Overview" section (near the end) that "The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period," giving a different owner and a different publication cadence for what reads as the same log.

findings.evidence: "If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee."
findings.fix: Replace the three "can apply" sentences with one sentence joining all conditions with "and," for example: "The stipend applies once the position is full-time, the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, and the request arrives before the benefit year ends."
findings.violation: Each of the first three sentences phrases its condition as independently sufficient ("the stipend can apply"), but the fourth sentence reverses that and requires all three conditions together, so a reader who stops after any one sentence draws the wrong conclusion.

findings.evidence: "Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email."
findings.fix: Remove the anecdote, or replace it with a general rule, for example: "If the assigned manager is unavailable, a designated backup reviewer completes the sign-off."
findings.violation: This sentence describes a specific, one-time scenario, a traveling manager and an uninformed backup reviewer, as though it were a routine step, so a reader cannot tell whether this delay is normal or an anecdote that does not belong in policy text.

findings.evidence: "The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist."
findings.fix: Rewrite in plain language and state the actual relationship, for example: "The manager approves items using the standard review checklist, with discretion to approve exceptions."
findings.violation: The sentence does not make clear whether the checklist governs approval or the manager's discretion overrides it, and its legal register breaks from the plain style used in the rest of the document.

findings.evidence: "Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time."
findings.fix: Replace with "The deposit reimburses the employee for costs already paid."
findings.violation: The sentence uses several extra words, "in order to" and "at this point in time", to express what "to reimburse the employee" would say directly.

findings.evidence: "You must keep your equipment in good working condition and we may ask for a brief photo check once a year."
findings.fix: Rewrite in third person to match the rest of the document, for example: "The employee must keep the equipment in good working condition, and the benefits team may request a brief photo check once a year."
findings.violation: This is the only sentence in the document written in second person, "you" and "we", while every other section refers to "the employee" and "the manager," so the voice shift may confuse a reader about who "we" refers to.

findings.evidence: "You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review."
findings.fix: Rename the section to reflect its actual content, for example "Monthly Reconciliation", rewrite it in third person, and replace the repeated phrase with a pronoun after its first use.
findings.violation: The section is titled "Terminology Notes" but defines no terms, describes a process instead, shifts again into second person, and repeats the phrase "stipend item" in three consecutive sentences without variation.

findings.evidence: "Also, you submit the request in the portal. You track its status there until the payment clears."
findings.fix: Remove this paragraph, or if status tracking is new information, move it into "How to Apply" and rewrite it in third person.
findings.violation: This repeats the submission process already described in "How to Apply" ("Employees start a stipend request in the benefits portal") without adding information, and continues the second-person voice that is inconsistent with the rest of the document.

findings.evidence: "Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt."
findings.fix: Delete this section, or merge its content into "How to Apply" if it is meant to summarize that section.
findings.violation: This section restates, in a single sentence, information already covered by "Eligibility" and "How to Apply," and its heading promises a sequence of steps but delivers only one sentence.

findings.evidence: "The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period. Staff can request a printed copy from the benefits team at any time."
findings.fix: Delete this duplicate section, or merge it with "Program Overview" and resolve the conflicting owner and cadence.
findings.violation: This section duplicates the heading and much of the wording of "Program Overview" near the top of the document, but changes who publishes the reimbursement log and how often, creating a direct contradiction, and its second sentence is a verbatim repeat of a sentence already used in "Program Overview."

findings.evidence: "The team then routes the request to the correct approver based on department."
findings.fix: State a single approval-routing process and use consistent terminology for the approver role across "How to Apply," "Approval Timeline," and "Program Coordination."
findings.violation: This describes the benefits team routing requests to a department-based approver, but "How to Apply" and "Approval Timeline" describe a single manager with a backup reviewer for absences and never mention departmental routing, so the document gives two different, unreconciled descriptions of who approves a request.

findings.evidence: "The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out."
findings.fix: State in "Approval Timeline" whether the finance office review for requests over 200 dollars falls inside the two-business-day window or is an additional step, and note any extra time it adds.
findings.violation: This introduces an additional review step and a dollar threshold that "Approval Timeline" never mentions, leaving it unclear whether the finance review happens inside the two-business-day window that section describes or adds time on top of it.

findings.evidence: "The benefits team publishes the vendor list each quarter."
findings.fix: Consolidate the periodic-publication statements into one section, for example "Publications," that lists each document, its owner, and its cadence once.
findings.violation: This is a third distinct periodic-publication claim in the document, after the reimbursement log in "Program Overview" and again in "Overview," and it is unclear whether the vendor list relates to those logs or is entirely separate.
